gauntlets-hold-attack-crowd-spacing.title: Moonlighter 2: Gauntlet Controls and Safer Crowd Spacing
gauntlets-hold-attack-crowd-spacing.description: Try held attacks instead of repeated presses, manage close-range positioning and compare a gauntlet switch without wasting an expedition.
gauntlets-hold-attack-crowd-spacing.intro: If Moonlighter 2's fist weapons feel exhausting or ineffective, first test holding the attack input instead of repeatedly pressing it, then shorten the sequence whenever positioning becomes unsafe. Players discussing gauntlets describe held attacks as a more comfortable way to use them. That input convenience does not remove the need to read enemies or create a safe position. This guide focuses on the weapon type's practical handling in ordinary rooms, rather than ranking every named gauntlet or promising that one build will outperform every sword and spear.

sections.heading: Test the input before replacing the weapon
paragraphs: Find a low-pressure place to verify how the attack behaves on your current platform and control arrangement. Press once, release, then compare a deliberate hold. Observe whether the sequence continues and what happens when you release the input. Do not begin the experiment while carrying an important late-run haul into a dangerous room. Your first objective is simply to learn the control behavior. A supported hold can reduce repetitive button presses, but you still need to know how quickly you can stop attacking and return attention to movement.

Repeat the comparison with the same weapon and equipment. Changing a perk or switching to another gauntlet during the input test makes the result harder to read. If holding does not behave as expected, inspect the current controls and any input assistance options rather than assuming a keyboard instruction transfers directly to your controller. Keep the action visible and deliberate. The useful outcome is a comfortable way to perform the ordinary attack sequence, not a reason to claim that every combat input can safely be held through an entire encounter.

sections.heading: Separate hand fatigue from combat efficiency
paragraphs: A weapon can be uncomfortable because you are pressing too often, and it can be ineffective because you are attacking from a bad position. These are different problems. If the hold test reduces hand strain but the character still takes avoidable damage, move to positioning rather than searching for another shortcut. Watch whether you keep attacking after the enemy begins its response or while another opponent approaches from outside your view. Less physical effort is helpful only if it leaves enough attention to notice when the attack should end.

Judge efficiency by the whole encounter. Finishing a room with reliable control and enough health for the next one is more useful than a brief impressive sequence followed by repeated trades. Avoid comparing only one large damage number with a weapon using a different rhythm. Include the time spent moving into reach, recovering from an unsafe exchange and restoring control after interruption. A practical comparison asks which weapon lets you complete your normal route comfortably, not which one looks most active while standing in front of a convenient target.

sections.heading: Enter close range with a clear exit
paragraphs: Before committing to a gauntlet sequence, notice where the nearest enemies are and which direction remains open. Moving into an opponent without checking the surrounding room can leave you surrounded before you finish the first sequence. Approach so that you can keep the main threat visible and avoid backing into an obstacle. The point is not to circle forever waiting for a perfect room. It is to choose a position from which stopping the attack still leaves a useful next action.

Start with a short commitment and release the input before the situation becomes crowded. Observe how the weapon returns control and whether you can move as intended. If you repeatedly take damage at the same point, end the sequence earlier on the next attempt. Do not treat the hold input as an obligation to continue. It is a convenient way to initiate repeated attacks; your decision about when to release remains part of the combat. Learning that stopping point makes the weapon feel controlled instead of automatic and difficult to interrupt.

sections.heading: Keep multiple enemies on one readable side
paragraphs: In a crowded room, divide attention deliberately. Identify the opponent that threatens your current position and consider whether another enemy can reach you during the attack. If you cannot keep both threats readable, reposition before extending the sequence. Fighting near scenery that blocks your movement can make a minor mistake much harder to recover from. Use open space when it is available and avoid chasing a nearly defeated enemy into a position where the rest of the room can attack from behind.

After a successful short exchange, pause long enough to read the next approach. This does not mean waiting passively through every encounter. It means preventing an input habit from making the next target selection for you. A held attack is comfortable when aimed at an appropriate opening, but it can become a liability if you continue after the room's geometry changes. If a group breaks apart, assess the new positions before pursuing. The safest target is not always the one with the least health if reaching it exposes you to several other attacks.

sections.heading: Add the weapon's extra action after the basics work
paragraphs: Read the current gauntlet description and identify any additional action or Berserk behavior available to your weapon. Test it separately from the held basic attack so you understand what changes and what resource or state the interface shows. Do not infer a fixed duration or a universal damage bonus from the name alone. Different weapons and upgrades can have their own descriptions, and a number copied from an incomplete table may not describe the item you currently own.

Once the basic sequence feels manageable, introduce the additional action at an opening you already recognize. Compare whether it helps finish the encounter or tempts you to stay committed longer than the position allows. If it produces a more dramatic sequence but causes the same unsafe trade, shorten the commitment before concluding that the weapon needs more upgrades. Your goal is to integrate the action into a route that works, not to prove that every available button must be used immediately whenever its icon becomes available.

sections.heading: Compare a switch over the same short route
paragraphs: If gauntlets remain uncomfortable after the input and spacing checks, compare another weapon you already understand. Keep the route and other equipment stable. Note where the alternate weapon solves the problem and where it introduces a different one. A longer-reaching attack may make one approach easier while demanding a different recovery rhythm. Do not turn a personal preference into a universal tier ranking. The correct choice for the next expedition is the one whose strengths you can actually use under the pressure your route creates.

Avoid spending a large reserve of upgrade materials merely to make the comparison feel fair on paper. First learn whether the alternate weapon's ordinary handling is attractive enough to justify a longer commitment. If it is, inspect the current upgrade requirements and plan the investment deliberately. If it is not, return to the gauntlet with the specific lesson you learned. Keeping the comparison small protects both your resources and the clarity of the result. You can improve a weapon decision without rebuilding the whole character after one frustrating room.

sections.heading: A departure check for the next expedition
paragraphs: Before leaving, confirm the input you intend to use, the point at which you will release it, and the room behavior that makes you reposition. Keep the weapon's additional action as a deliberate choice rather than a reflex. If hand fatigue returns, take a break and reassess the control arrangement instead of forcing more repetitions. Comfortable handling should support play, and no weapon ranking is worth turning an optional action game into a painful exercise in button pressing.

Are gauntlets automatically bad because they require close positioning? No; judge the encounters you can complete reliably. Does holding attack make you safe from surrounding enemies? No; releasing and moving remain important. Must you switch to a spear because someone else prefers it? No. Test the held input, keep threats readable, choose short commitments and compare alternatives only when you can name the problem they would solve. Those steps produce a practical weapon choice while leaving the actual dungeon and shop decisions at the center of the session.

keeper-storage-quick-stash-materials.title: Moonlighter 2: Keeper Storage and Quick-Stash Checks
keeper-storage-quick-stash-materials.description: Organize a town storage transfer, protect upgrade materials from accidental selling, and verify what a stash command actually moved.
keeper-storage-quick-stash-materials.intro: Before your next Moonlighter 2 expedition, separate the materials you intend to keep from the items you intend to sell, then verify the result of any storage transfer on both sides of the inventory. Do not assume there is a universal quick-stash key that works in every menu or on every platform. Use the command shown by your current interface. This guide addresses the practical Keeper-storage question as a town preparation routine: clear enough space for the next trip while preserving resources you already decided to reserve. It does not promise remote storage access from every dungeon room.

sections.heading: Decide what belongs in storage before transferring
paragraphs: Begin with a concrete goal for the next trip. You might be collecting resources for a planned equipment purchase, exploring a new area, or making a selling run. The goal determines which items you should preserve. Look at the current recipe or purchase requirement in your game and note the names and quantities you still need. A material that sold well in an earlier session may now be part of the upgrade you want. Storage organization should reflect the next decision, not a permanent rule that every expensive item must always be sold.

Create three practical categories in your own notes: reserve, sell, and undecided. You do not need a spreadsheet or a new sorting feature to use them. Reserve items already have a purpose, selling stock is available for your shop plan, and undecided items need another look before disposal. Keep the last category small. If you cannot identify an item's role, read its current description and compare it with the equipment you are actually pursuing. Moving it out of sight without a reason can be as confusing as leaving it in the backpack.

sections.heading: Read the visible transfer command
paragraphs: Open the relevant storage interaction and inspect the controls displayed in that screen. A button used to move an item in one menu should not be assumed to perform the same action everywhere else. Check whether the prompt describes one item, a stack, or a broader transfer. If no bulk command is shown, use the normal individual transfer rather than trying shortcuts suggested for a different game or platform. The practical requirement is a reliable result, not the shortest possible input sequence on your first attempt.

Test with an ordinary item whose before-and-after count is easy to recognize. Note its backpack quantity and its storage quantity, activate the displayed command once, and inspect both counts again. If only part of a stack moved, read any quantity selection that appeared. If nothing moved, check the highlight and any capacity message. This small trial answers what the command does in your current menu without putting an important reserved material at risk. Once the behavior is clear, apply it to the rest of the planned transfer.

sections.heading: Preserve recipe materials before arranging shop stock
paragraphs: Move reserved materials deliberately and confirm that you can identify them in storage afterward. Keep a note of the upgrade they are reserved for if several projects use similar resources. Do not rely solely on an icon or an assumed sorting position. When you next inspect a recipe, compare its requirement with the current counts rather than remembering the total from before the last expedition. Materials can be spent or moved between visits, and the useful number is the one present at the moment you decide to craft or buy.

Only after reserves are accounted for should you prepare the items intended for selling. This order reduces the chance of placing a useful material into a selling workflow by habit. It does not mean every unidentified item deserves permanent protection. Review the undecided group with a specific question: is there a near-term use that makes keeping this item worthwhile? If the answer is unclear, keep a modest reserve while you learn rather than making a large irreversible sale because a generic price table says the item is valuable.

sections.heading: Handle partial transfers without repeating blind inputs
paragraphs: If a transfer stops unexpectedly, inspect both sides of the interaction before pressing again. Look for a full container, a quantity prompt, a changed selection, or another visible explanation. Repeated confirmation can make it harder to determine which action moved the item and may target a different row after the first transfer succeeds. Work in small batches until the interface feels predictable. Efficiency comes from understanding the command, not from sending more inputs while the result remains unclear.

When a stack seems missing, search the destination as well as the backpack. Sorting changes can place it somewhere you did not expect. Read the item name and check counts instead of concluding that a familiar icon disappearing means an item was destroyed. If the visible counts still cannot explain the result, stop moving valuable resources and record the interaction. Include the platform, item, starting count, command used, and observed destination. That is a useful description of a possible issue without inventing a recovery method or claiming a known bug.

sections.heading: Prepare a departure inventory you can understand
paragraphs: After storage and selling preparation, inspect the backpack as if you were about to leave immediately. Ask whether every remaining item has a reason to accompany the trip. Do not carry reserved materials merely because you forgot to finish the transfer. At the same time, avoid removing resources that the game's current preparation screen indicates you need. A clean inventory is not an empty inventory; it is one whose contents make sense for the next objective. Preserve the tools your actual run depends on and clear the items that do not belong there.

Use the next return to town as a feedback check. Did the inventory fill sooner than expected? Did you discover that a supposedly spare material was needed? Did a transfer consume more attention than the dungeon itself? Adjust the categories accordingly. You do not need to organize the entire collection after every room. A short consistent routine at town is easier to maintain: inspect the next objective, reserve materials, transfer deliberately, prepare selling stock, and verify departure space. That rhythm supports the game's dungeon-to-shop loop without turning preparation into its own endless task.

sections.heading: Know what this method does not establish
paragraphs: Can you quick-stash directly to the Keeper from anywhere? Do not assume it; check the interaction available in your current location. Is there a confirmed universal keyboard shortcut? This guide does not provide one because the visible controls and platform matter. Does storing a material guarantee every crafting interface will count it automatically? Verify the requirement display where you intend to use it rather than assuming remote access. These distinctions prevent a convenient town workflow from becoming an unsupported claim about every inventory system in the game.

The useful outcome is simple: you know what was moved, where it went, why you kept it, and what space remains for the next trip. If a shortcut is visible and behaves as expected, use it after a small test. If it is absent or unclear, normal transfers still accomplish the preparation goal. Keep the steps that prevent mistakes and remove the unnecessary administration. A good storage routine should make it easier to return to exploration and shop decisions, while protecting the resources you already chose to save for something worthwhile.

moonlighter-2-bloblets-guide.title: Moonlighter 2 Bloblets: How to Rescue, Adopt and Activate Them
moonlighter-2-bloblets-guide.description: How Bloblets work in Moonlighter 2: earn the currency in dungeon Bloblet rooms, adopt at the pet seller, then hold Pet in the shop to trigger the effect.
moonlighter-2-bloblets-guide.intro: Bloblets are the small shop companions Moonlighter 2 added in the Blob-Life Balance Update on May 20, 2026, and they remain one of the least explained systems in version 1.0. An October Steam discussion thread asked the question many players run into: the shop describes effects such as more tips for a short time or better sales for a few items, but when do they start, and how do you trigger them? The answer from other players is that you pet the Bloblet in your shop. This guide walks through the whole loop as the developers described it, from earning the currency in the dungeons to adopting at the pet seller in Tresna and timing the effect on the shop floor.

sections.heading: Where Bloblets come from
paragraphs: The Blob-Life patch notes describe Bloblets as a new system that affects both parts of the game loop. In the dungeon, you complete Bloblet challenges to earn a new currency. Back in Tresna, you exchange that currency for new Bloblets at the pet seller, which the same notes list as the vendor where you rescue and adopt Bloblets. The May patch notes name the seller Zane Jane, while the version 1.0 Hotfix 1 notes refer to Hazy Jane, the name our character page uses.

Hotfix 1 also confirms that the challenge lives inside the dungeon: it fixed the dungeon music not restarting after the Bloblet room if you left before its track ended. In practice, a Bloblet challenge is a room on your route, not a menu in town. When one appears, judge it the way you would judge any optional node, against the health you have left and the relics already in your backpack. The same hotfix fixed a loss of player input when talking to Hazy Jane during later stages of the game, so if the vendor froze your controls before September 14, 2026, update the game before assuming your save is broken.

sections.heading: How to activate a Bloblet in the shop
paragraphs: The Blob-Life notes say that once you unlock Bloblets at the pet seller, you can equip a Bloblet for the shop run, and it grants special effects until you close the shop. What the notes do not spell out, and what confused the October thread, is the trigger. Players answered that you use the Bloblet by petting it, and one reply added that this step is not covered in the tutorial, which explains why so many people equip one and never see anything happen.

One of the official Steam store screenshots shows the interaction directly. A companion named Sir Edwin rests on a cushion in the shop with a Pet (Hold) prompt above it. The tooltip at the bottom of the screen says the next 3 relics you place in a display case gain 10 of the value marked by a sparkle icon. So the input is a hold, not a tap. Walk up to the Bloblet, hold the interact button shown on screen until the prompt completes, and read the effect text: it tells you exactly what the next stretch of your shop will receive.

sections.heading: Time the pet, not just the equip
paragraphs: The developers describe the bonuses as temporary, naming increased relic value and better customer tips as examples. That makes timing more important than the choice of companion. Sir Edwin's effect counts the next three relics placed in a display case, so the sensible order is to pet first and then place the relics you most want to boost. If you fill the cases with cheap filler right after petting, the count is spent on items that barely matter.

The thread starter described other effect texts in two shapes: a short window of more tips, and a set number of items that sell for more money. A window effect is wasted in an empty shop. Wait until customers are already browsing or lining up before you hold the prompt. A count-based effect is the opposite: it does not expire while you wait, so line up your most valuable relics first. The same screenshot shows a Tip Value counter in the top-left corner of the shop screen, which is the easiest place to check whether a tip effect is actually doing something during your session.

sections.heading: Combine Bloblets with Aromas and price hints
paragraphs: Aromas arrived in the same Blob-Life update. After you sell some relics at a Cheap price, a machine in the shop drops a random Aroma from three possible options, and you can apply it to a showcase for passive effects until the end of the shop run. When the developers ran a shopkeeping contest after the update, they explicitly asked players to put Bloblet effects and Aromas to work together, so treat them as one shop-floor toolkit rather than two separate systems.

The update also added price hints. When you know the price ranges above and below the one you are setting, an indicator shows whether it lands in Cheap, Perfect, Expensive or Overpriced, and a question mark appears when you do not know the ranges yet. A hint also appears when a price is so far from fair that no customer will be interested. Keep that discipline even with a Bloblet active: a value or tip bonus cannot rescue a relic that nobody will buy at the price on its tag.

sections.heading: More room for Bloblets as the shop grows
paragraphs: Shop Level 4 also came with the Blob-Life update. The September 2, 2026 version 1.0 launch post then added Shop Level 5, which gives you an additional Bloblet slot so you can bring more companions along, plus a new cosmetic placement slot for another decoration. Neither post prints the total number of slots, the unlock cost, or how many Bloblets exist in total, so do not trust a guide that quotes those numbers as official.

sections.heading: Collecting them all: what the achievements show
paragraphs: In the Early Access progress post that previewed the feature, the developers named skins such as Rumblet, Guyblob Threepup and Mr. Spots while the assets were still marked as work in progress, and said the skins would increase item value and alter sell prices. Treat those names as previews. If the collector achievements matter to you, take Bloblet rooms whenever the route and your health allow it, and spend the currency at the pet seller between runs instead of letting it pile up.

sections.heading: Quick Bloblet checklist
bullets: Clear Bloblet rooms in dungeons to earn the Bloblet currency.
Adopt at the pet seller in Tresna (Hazy Jane in the Hotfix 1 notes).
Equip a Bloblet for the shop run; its effect lasts until you close the shop.
Hold the Pet prompt to trigger it. The tutorial does not explain this step.
For count-based effects, pet first, then place your best relics.
For time-window effects, pet when customers are already in the shop.
Shop Level 5 adds one more Bloblet slot, according to the version 1.0 launch post.

moonlighter-2-stuck-enemies-softlock-gui.title: Moonlighter 2 Stuck Enemies and Softlocks: How to Protect a Run
moonlighter-2-stuck-enemies-softlock-gui.description: Flying enemies that never land, rooms that will not open, zipline lockups: what Moonlighter 2 players report in November 2026 and how to protect your backpack.
moonlighter-2-stuck-enemies-softlock-gui.intro: If you have had to abandon a Moonlighter 2 run three quarters of the way through, you are not alone. Since late October, the busiest threads on the game's Steam discussion board have been about run-ending bugs: enemies stuck in the air, enemies you cannot hit, and rooms that stay locked after the last enemy is gone. A November 2 review describes exactly that case, a flying enemy that stopped attacking and would not land while the player had run out of gun ammo. As of November 4, 2026, the newest patch notes on Steam are still the version 1.0 Hotfix 1 from September 14, 2026. Until something newer ships, the useful question is how to stop a bug from costing you the backpack.

sections.heading: What players are reporting right now
paragraphs: These are player reports from Steam reviews and discussions posted in late October and early November 2026. They are not confirmed by the developers, and some may depend on platform or timing, but they come up often enough to plan around.
bullets: Flying enemies stuck in the air that stop attacking and never land, leaving the room locked.
Enemies standing on the floor next to Will that cannot be hit by the melee weapon or the gun, with the gun aiming at other enemies instead.
Rooms with no enemies left that still do not let you progress, reported two or three levels before the boss.
In Aeolia, riding the ziplines in quick succession or with many enemies on screen, after which Will could not attack, dodge or interact.
Getting stuck in a falling animation in the Greed arena with a backpack full of relics.
The Kalina Night Realm boss getting stuck in his ground pound animation with the damage pool beneath him.
Controller drift in menus, and on keyboard and mouse the roll occasionally stopping working.
A console player reporting that the A and + buttons stopped working after porting home from a boss fight.

sections.heading: What Hotfix 1 already fixed
paragraphs: Before you assume your problem is new, make sure you are on Hotfix 1. The September 14 notes fixed a spot in Kalina where players could fall out of the map with no way to recover the run, Will getting stuck behind an obstacle in the Gallery area, the CH4 Turret getting stuck in its shooting animation after being tased, spearhead projectiles freezing in midair when reaching Will, and Sergeant Roberto not reacting when shot from a distance. It also restored Barrier Blessing shield charges when retrying a dungeon. The developers said they would bring these fixes to the console versions as soon as possible and then assess balancing and gameplay.

Earlier Early Access patches also addressed similar failures, including a soft lock when stepping into the Greed Colosseum and The Curator boss sometimes stopping responding and becoming invincible. The pattern matters: the team has fixed bugs when reports named the exact enemy, spot and situation. None of the reports listed above appears in a patch note yet, so for now you need a plan for when one happens to you.

sections.heading: Rule one: the pendant is your bug insurance
paragraphs: Compare that with the cost of a death. On Easy, Normal and Hard, dying halves the quality of every relic in the backpack. On Expert you lose those relics outright, and on Hardcore a death costs your progress and starts the journey over. We have not found an official statement about what abandoning a run does to your backpack, and players who abandoned describe it as losing the run. Treat the pendant as the known-safe exit. If an enemy is hovering and not attacking, or the doors stay shut after the last enemy falls, give it a short moment, try the obvious answers once, and then pendant out if the bag is worth more than the rest of the run.

sections.heading: Keep gun ammo for flying enemies
paragraphs: The gun rides alongside your melee weapon, and it is the main way to hit anything that is not on the ground. The November 2 review that sparked this guide ended because the player had no ammo left when the flying enemy got stuck. Going into later rooms, especially in a region with flyers, keep a few shots in reserve instead of emptying the gun on targets your melee weapon can already reach.

This is not a guarantee. One discussion report describes an enemy on the floor that neither the weapon nor the gun could hit, so ammo will not save every broken room. It does turn some stuck-enemy situations from a forced exit into a few seconds of shooting, and it costs you nothing in fights you would have won anyway.

sections.heading: Routes and terrain to treat carefully
paragraphs: The dungeon map is your best planning tool. The official screenshot of Aeolia's Zephyr Fields map shows a legend for chests, events, potions, the blacksmith, recipes, elite enemies, minibosses, bosses and perk rooms. Before you enter a section with an elite or a miniboss, decide in advance where you will pendant out if something goes wrong. One player in the bugs thread also noted that the potion symbol on the map does not match the icon in the map key, so read the node itself, not only the legend.

Zephyr Fields is the zipline region, with wind traps and ziplines throughout. Given the report of a lockup after chaining ziplines quickly with many enemies on screen, clear the enemies around a zipline before you ride it and do not trigger several in a row at full speed. Treat the Greed arena and the Kalina Night Realm boss with the same caution when you are carrying a valuable bag. The safest moment to extract is before the door, not after the bug.

sections.heading: Fix the technical side first
paragraphs: Some run losses are crashes rather than logic bugs, and recent reviews mention long loading times and crashes during dungeon runs on PC and Steam Deck. The pinned Tech Support and Known Issues thread from 11 bit studios lists the official steps. If the update is not showing, exit and fully close Steam, then relaunch. For freezing, lag or crashes on PC, reinstall your GPU driver cleanly with Display Driver Uninstaller, disable overlays such as Steam, Discord, GeForce Experience or AMD Radeon, turn off overclocking tools, and verify the integrity of the game files.

On Steam Deck, the thread recommends setting all graphics options to Low and restarting the game, with Antialiasing set to FSR3 and the upscaling preset on Balanced or Quality. If you use a PS4 or PS5 controller but see Xbox button prompts, disable Steam Input. On PC, Hotfix 1 also added a DirectX 11 and DirectX 12 option, which is worth comparing if crashes keep ending runs.

sections.heading: Report it so it can be fixed
paragraphs: The pinned thread asks players to email techsupport@11bitstudios.com rather than relying on forum replies, and says reports do not have to be written in English. Include the platform, the dungeon and floor, the enemy or terrain involved, your weapon, gun and active perks, and what you did right before the bug. Hotfix 1's notes name specific enemies and exact spots, which suggests that precise reports are the ones that turn into fixes.

senda-poison-scarabastion-fair-build.title: Moonlighter 2: Senda Poison and Scarabastion Build Checks
senda-poison-scarabastion-fair-build.description: Retest Senda poison, Scarabastion defense and weapon behavior before investing in a boss build, with a practical practice sequence.
senda-poison-scarabastion-fair-build.intro: A boss build is only useful when its central interaction behaves the way you think it does. Moonlighter 2's version 1.0 Hotfix 1 fixes Senda taking no poison damage from gadget shots in his second phase, removes unintended boss invincibility from Scarabastion, and corrects several weapon behaviors. Those changes remain important for players returning around the late-October platform discussions, even though the PC hotfix itself dates to September. This guide turns those specific issues into a combat testing routine, then explains how to choose a dependable setup without relying on an exploit or an outdated description.

sections.heading: Confirm the build and platform first
paragraphs: Before entering a difficult encounter, inspect the current equipment and the version available on your platform. A PC correction and a console rollout are not automatically simultaneous. Check your installed update normally, then read the item and weapon descriptions present in your own game. Do not assume an old screenshot or a discussion from a different platform describes your current behavior. The practical objective is to understand what your setup does today, not to reproduce a successful-looking video whose build and update state are unknown.

Write down the role of the weapon, gadget, and armor you intend to use. Keep the explanation concrete: reach for safer pokes, a status effect you want to apply, or defense that lets you recover from a mistake. If the entire plan depends on receiving no damage under a bugged condition, replace that assumption before testing anything else. Stable fundamentals make later comparisons meaningful. Otherwise, an apparent performance improvement may simply reflect a disappearing exploit rather than a genuine change in how effectively you are playing the encounter.

sections.heading: Separate reaching phase two from testing poison
paragraphs: The Senda fix concerns poison damage from gadget shots in his second phase. First build a reliable way to reach that phase with enough resources to observe the interaction. Do not spend every attempt chasing a perfect opening in the first phase if the question you need answered occurs later. Use the attack patterns you understand, keep punish sequences short, and avoid consuming the tools intended for your test before the relevant phase begins. The preparation should support a clear observation, not merely a fast first half.

During the second phase, make a deliberate gadget shot when you can see the target and the relevant feedback. Watch for the status and damage behavior the game displays. A miss, a blocked shot, and a landed shot with no expected effect are different outcomes. Avoid calling the interaction broken because one hurried attempt produced unclear feedback. Repeat only when you have a safe opening and enough resources to compare. This is a testing method, not a promise that poison alone will carry the encounter or ignore its other mechanics.

sections.heading: Replace Scarabastion invincibility with a defensive routine
paragraphs: Hotfix 1 corrects an issue where equipping Scarabastion could make players invincible during boss fights. A build built around that behavior should be treated as outdated. Equip the armor only for the properties its current description and behavior actually provide. Test a normal incoming attack in a controlled situation if you need to understand your survivability. Do not repeatedly provoke the boss expecting the old state to reappear. Learning defense while assuming you cannot be hurt creates habits that become expensive the moment the exploit is gone.

Give yourself a simple defensive sequence: identify the incoming attack, move or defend deliberately, wait for the complete string, and take a brief opening. If damage rises after updating, compare your play to that sequence before spending heavily on replacement gear. You may need to stop trading through attacks rather than rebuild every equipment slot. Once the encounter feels readable, increase aggression gradually. The best defensive setup is one that supports mistakes you can recover from, while leaving you enough control to avoid repeating the same mistake throughout the fight.

sections.heading: Read the weapon after the correction
paragraphs: The second greatsword's sharpness drain is among the corrected behaviors. If you use that weapon, inspect the current sharpness behavior across a short, repeatable set of actions. Compare the display before attacking, after the sequence, and after any normal recovery the game provides. Do not infer a full efficiency ranking from one long fight with different enemies. Your first question is whether you understand the cost of the attacks you prefer. Resource awareness matters more than preserving a familiar combo that now spends differently.

The Vow also receives a description correction. Read the new wording before choosing it for a particular effect. A tooltip correction can change the information available to the player without necessarily meaning that every part of the weapon was redesigned. Compare what the description says with what you can observe, and keep uncertainty narrow if a detail remains unclear. Avoid adding an invented multiplier or hidden synergy to fill the gap. A weapon you can explain in plain terms is easier to use well than one selected for an impressive but unsupported promise.

sections.heading: Keep perk experiments away from a valuable attempt
paragraphs: A crash involving a specific Wound and Ignite combination is addressed in the PC hotfix. If your old setup was affected, update before reproducing the combination, then test it in a modest activity rather than at the end of a precious run. Keep other equipment constant while checking whether the previous failure returns. If a crash persists, note the exact perks and sequence. A report that identifies the combination is more useful than repeatedly changing unrelated graphics settings because the game closed during combat.

Once the combination behaves reliably, judge its combat value on the same practical route used for your baseline. Does it help you finish safely, or does it encourage standing in danger to chase a theoretical effect? Separate technical reliability from usefulness. A fixed crash does not automatically make a perk pairing the strongest choice, and a modest damage improvement is not worthwhile if it repeatedly disrupts the defense you just learned. Build around a sequence you can execute when the boss stops behaving like a stationary target.

sections.heading: Bring a complete plan to the next boss attempt
paragraphs: Before returning to Senda, check four things: the installed update, the intended gadget interaction, the armor's real defensive role, and the weapon resource behavior. If any one remains unclear, test that component briefly before risking the full attempt. In the fight, aim to reach phase two consistently, take clear gadget openings, and keep enough attention on defense to see what happened. Do not add several new mechanics at once because an earlier attempt reached the final stretch.

Afterward, record one change for the next try. Keep what worked and replace the weakest decision, whether that was early resource spending, an unsafe punish, or dependence on outdated armor behavior. A trustworthy build does not need a spectacular claim behind every slot. It needs predictable actions that work together: a weapon you can manage, a gadget used at a readable opening, and defense that functions on the updated game. Those are the ingredients that make a returning player's next session feel like progress rather than a disagreement with last month's advice.

infinite-vault-threshold-budget-route.title: Moonlighter 2: Build a Safer Infinite Vault Threshold Run
infinite-vault-threshold-budget-route.description: Plan your next Infinite Endless Vault threshold around its gold target, equipment and extraction decisions instead of chasing every room.
infinite-vault-threshold-budget-route.intro: Moonlighter 2's Infinite Endless Vault asks for a different mindset from an ordinary exploratory trip. After the main story, its increasingly demanding thresholds must each be completed in a single run; missing the required gold resets progress for that threshold. That rule makes reliable decisions more valuable than an exciting start. Returning players comparing versions and performance in late October should first ensure the game runs reliably, then plan around the target their own screen displays. The route below is an analytical planning method, not a claim that one equipment combination guarantees every threshold.

sections.heading: Read the current target before choosing equipment
paragraphs: Begin by checking the threshold and required gold shown in your game. Do not copy a target from a screenshot without checking whether it represents the same stage. The required amount is the objective that determines success, while an impressive inventory or a powerful weapon is only a means to reach it. Make a short note of the target and the equipment you intend to bring. This gives you a useful reference when a run ends short and helps explain whether the failure came from insufficient earnings or avoidable losses.

Choose equipment you already understand for the first attempt. A new weapon can improve a later route, but learning its reach and recovery while carrying a valuable run adds risk. Ask which part of the previous attempt failed: clearing enemies, preserving health, or producing enough value. Address that constraint directly. If fights are already comfortable, changing every combat tool is unlikely to solve poor route decisions. If you lose health in ordinary rooms, a more ambitious earning plan will not matter unless the character survives long enough to execute it.

sections.heading: Separate essential loot from tempting detours
paragraphs: When entering a section, decide what would make the next room worth the cost. A detour can offer more value but also consume health, time, and concentration. Assess it using the current condition of the run rather than the feeling that every unopened path must contain an upgrade. The threshold requirement creates a clear goal; it does not require proving that you can clear every encounter while injured. Keep track of the resources you still need and avoid taking an unnecessary risk simply because the previous few rooms went well.

Use a simple decision sequence at each safe pause. Review health, the value you have accumulated, available resources, and the route you can actually follow. If you are still short, choose the next activity with a specific reason for expecting useful progress. If you are close, protect what you have earned instead of extending the run for an unclear marginal gain. This advice does not invent a universal extraction shortcut or a hidden threshold multiplier. It is a way to align ordinary dungeon choices with the explicit single-run requirement.

sections.heading: Build a small record of failed attempts
paragraphs: After a failed threshold, write one sentence describing the decisive moment. Perhaps you lost too much health in an early encounter, followed a detour that did not pay off, or reached the end without enough value. Avoid the unhelpful explanation that the whole build was bad unless you can identify where it failed. Keep the same equipment for another attempt if the major mistake was clearly a route decision. A consistent baseline makes improvement visible and reduces the urge to spend resources on changes that address the wrong problem.

When a combat issue repeats, isolate the enemy action that causes it. Practice reading that action in a lower-pressure context where possible, then return with a shorter punish or more deliberate spacing. Do not judge a weapon only by a strong opening burst. Ask whether it remains manageable when you must reposition, recover, or deal with several opponents. A run that finishes a little more slowly can still be the better threshold strategy if it preserves enough health to continue earning instead of collapsing near the finish.

sections.heading: Protect stability before risking a valuable run
paragraphs: The PC Hotfix 1 provides DirectX 11 and DirectX 12 options. If your current problem is a crash or repeated severe hitching, compare those options before committing another important attempt. Keep resolution and the route constant, restart when required, and record which API completes the same activity reliably. The presence of a selector does not mean either API is universally superior. Your goal is a stable environment in which a failed threshold reflects a gameplay decision rather than a renderer test conducted at the worst possible moment.

Do not switch on an unfamiliar permanent-risk mode merely to compare performance. Use a suitable existing profile and a modest activity for the technical check. If an issue occurs only during a particular transition, test that transition rather than wandering around town and declaring the problem fixed. Keep platform and patch information attached to your notes. A console patch number circulating in a late-October discussion does not automatically describe the PC build, and the September PC hotfix should not be advertised as a newly released November update.

sections.heading: Upgrade the bottleneck rather than everything
paragraphs: Once you understand why a threshold failed, choose one improvement. If your attacks leave you exposed, practice or equipment familiarity may help before an expensive purchase. If you repeatedly arrive short despite comfortable combat, inspect your earning decisions and any relevant upgrades available in your own progression. The version 1.0 postgame includes further equipment and shop-related unlocks, but that does not mean every unlock is required for the next threshold. Read costs and effects in the current interface instead of buying by category name alone.

Keep a reserve for the activity you intend to do next. Spending all available resources on an experimental setup can leave you unable to return to the reliable option you just abandoned. Compare a new choice over a short controlled route, then decide whether its benefit is clear enough for another threshold attempt. Your criterion should be practical: does it reduce the failure that actually ended the previous run? A small targeted upgrade with an obvious role is easier to evaluate than a completely new loadout assembled from conflicting recommendations.

sections.heading: Know what a successful practice run teaches
paragraphs: A useful attempt produces information even if it fails the target. You should know where the earnings fell behind, where health became critical, and which optional decision you would change next time. Keep the notes brief enough to read before the next departure. The goal is to improve the route, not to turn the game into unpaid administration. Once a threshold is completed, read the next requirement afresh and do not assume the previous margin will remain sufficient as difficulty rises.

The Infinite Vault becomes more manageable when every decision serves a visible objective. Confirm the target, bring familiar equipment, take detours for a reason, preserve the run when it is nearly complete, and change only the bottleneck after a failure. That approach will not remove the challenge or guarantee a clear. It does make setbacks understandable, which is what lets the next expedition begin with a better plan instead of the same hopeful equipment and the same unclear route.

moonlighter-2-hotfix-1-retest-guide.title: Moonlighter 2 Hotfix 1 Guide: Stability, Quest, and Dungeon Fixes
moonlighter-2-hotfix-1-retest-guide.description: A practical retest route for Moonlighter 2 Hotfix 1: DirectX 11 or 12, the Weapon Mastery marker, tutorial freezes, Senda, and dungeon recovery.
moonlighter-2-hotfix-1-retest-guide.intro: Moonlighter 2 Hotfix 1 addresses stability, progression, enemies, weapons, armor, dungeons, and text issues reported around the version 1.0 release. The most useful way to apply it is to update first, choose one symptom, and retest the exact activity that failed. This guide turns the patch notes into a safe checklist without treating a fixed bug as a new strategy.

sections.heading: Install the patch before repeating a risky run
paragraphs: Close the game and let your platform complete the update before loading a valuable save. The patch addresses issues that could crash after a main quest, freeze while returning to Tresna during the tutorial, or leave a dungeon run unrecoverable. Those are different failure points, so write down where the original problem occurred. A title-screen version check, if your build displays one, is a better baseline than assuming an update downloaded because the client was open.

After updating, load the same profile and repeat only the action connected to the original symptom. Do not immediately delete a save, reinstall, or abandon a quest. If the failure no longer occurs, continue normally and keep a note of the new build. If it persists, capture the quest name, location, platform, and the last action before the freeze or crash. That makes a remaining issue distinguishable from an old report reproduced on an outdated install.

sections.heading: Choose DirectX 11 or DirectX 12 with a controlled comparison
paragraphs: Hotfix 1 adds a choice between DirectX 11 and DirectX 12 because some instability and performance problems may be related to the graphics API. There is no universal best option in the notes. Start with the setting currently selected, play a repeatable section, and record whether the issue is a crash, a frame-rate drop, or a hitch during a transition. Then switch APIs, restart if the game requests it, and repeat the same section with the same resolution and graphics settings.

Do not change the API, resolution, upscaler, frame cap, and graphics preset all at once. If several variables change, a smoother run cannot tell you which setting mattered. Keep the first configuration written down so you can restore it. A result on one GPU does not prove the other API is slower or less stable on every PC. If neither option changes the symptom, preserve the log and report the hardware and driver state instead of repeatedly toggling settings without a controlled test.

sections.heading: Recover the tutorial return to Tresna
paragraphs: The patch fixes a loading-screen freeze that could happen when returning to Tresna during the tutorial. If your tutorial save previously stopped on that transition, update and try the normal return once before changing files. Wait for the transition to finish and avoid force-closing the game while the storage indicator or loading screen is still active. If the town loads correctly, check the quest journal and confirm that the tutorial step advanced before leaving the area.

If the loading screen still hangs, note whether the freeze happens every time or only on one save. Record the platform, API selection on PC, and whether you changed the route or equipment before returning. Do not assume a later-game loading freeze has the same cause as this tutorial-specific case. A precise report keeps the known fix narrow and helps identify whether another transition issue remains.

sections.heading: Use the Weapon Mastery marker as navigation, not a quest reset
paragraphs: Hotfix 1 corrects the Weapon Mastery quest marker when it pointed to the wrong location. Reopen the journal after updating, select the quest, and follow the current marker rather than an old screenshot or community route. If the marker leads somewhere unexpected, compare the displayed quest text with the map label and check whether another objective is active. A marker correction changes navigation guidance; it does not imply that the quest requirements or reward were redesigned.

When a quest remains incomplete, identify the exact stage and the interaction the journal asks for. Revisit the corrected destination, inspect nearby interactable objects, and check whether the objective text changes. Avoid repeating every earlier step unless the journal says to. If the marker and objective disagree after the patch, preserve a screenshot of both and report the mismatch. That is more useful than restarting the whole quest and potentially obscuring the broken state.

sections.heading: Test the Babyl and Spark route without creating another blocker
paragraphs: The patch fixes Babyl sometimes being duplicated, which could make Spark almost impossible to reach when Babyl had not yet been unlocked. This is a dependency and navigation edge case. If you are approaching that part of the story, check the journal and unlock state before moving between the characters. Do not assume that seeing a duplicate means you have unlocked the intended route; confirm the relevant interaction and objective state in the menu.

If Spark still cannot be reached, record whether Babyl is unlocked, how many copies or markers appear, and which objective is active. Use the main quest path shown in the current build and avoid deleting local progress to work around a world-state issue. The patch note describes the specific combination that caused the obstruction. It does not say that all character interactions or every blocked door are related to this fix.

sections.heading: Retest Senda and other named enemy fixes
paragraphs: Hotfix 1 fixes Senda not taking poison damage from gadget shots during the second phase. To verify it, reach the second phase, use the relevant poison gadget, and watch for the game’s damage response. Do not test in the first phase and conclude that the second-phase correction failed. Keep the gadget, target phase, and attack sequence consistent if you compare attempts.

The same patch changes several other named cases: Sergeant Roberto should react when shot from a distance; the Chapter 4 turret should no longer stay in its firing animation after being tased; and tased Electric Slimes should not continue dealing electric-field damage. Test each in its stated context. A turret that was not tased, a slime whose status expired, or a close-range shot on Roberto does not reproduce the exact issue described.

sections.heading: Protect a run from dungeon-specific edge cases
paragraphs: The update fixes a spot in Kalina where Will could fall out of the map and become stuck, and another Gallery obstacle that could trap him. It also restores Barrier Blessing shield charges when retrying a dungeon and fixes certain legendary-chest rewards after miniboss victories. These changes affect different parts of a run: geometry, retry state, and reward generation. Check which one matches your situation before leaving or restarting.

After a miniboss, open the reward chest and confirm the reward appears before moving on. When retrying with Barrier Blessing, inspect the displayed shield state before taking another encounter. If a character becomes stuck, try the normal movement and camera controls once, then record the exact obstacle and room rather than repeatedly forcing the same position. A route guide should note the fixed obstruction only when it has been retested on the patched build.

sections.heading: Check the remaining weapon, armor, and text corrections
paragraphs: Hotfix 1 corrects a crash caused by a specific combination of Wound and Ignite perks, spearhead projectiles freezing in midair when reaching Will, the second greatsword’s sharpness drain, and a mismatch between The Vow’s description and behavior. It also fixes an invincibility edge case during boss fights after equipping Scarabastion. These are not blanket changes to every perk, weapon, or armor effect.

If you use one of those combinations, note your loadout before testing and change one item at a time. Read the current description for The Vow rather than copying an older tooltip. The update also corrects placeholder/debug text and a misspelling in the Shared Secret relic description in English and Portuguese. Text corrections can help identify the installed build, but they do not necessarily change the relic’s underlying function.

sections.heading: A clean post-hotfix checklist
paragraphs: Update; back up your normal save through the platform’s supported method; choose one symptom; repeat the matching quest, enemy, or dungeon event; and note the current graphics API if you are on PC. Confirm quest completion in the journal, check a reward before leaving its room, and avoid mixing several settings changes into one test. If the game still fails, preserve the save and record the exact steps rather than wiping progress.

The patch is broad, but each fix is specific. Treat the corrected Weapon Mastery marker as a marker fix, the Senda note as a second-phase poison case, and the loading freeze as a tutorial return issue. That precision lets you benefit from Hotfix 1 without inventing a new route or assuming every similar-looking problem has already been solved.

moonlighter-2-directx-stutter-test.title: Moonlighter 2 DirectX 11 vs 12: A Safe Stutter and Crash Test
moonlighter-2-directx-stutter-test.description: Compare Moonlighter 2 DirectX 11 and 12 after Hotfix 1 with a repeatable PC test for crashes, loading, frame pacing, and graphics settings.
moonlighter-2-directx-stutter-test.intro: Moonlighter 2 Hotfix 1 adds a DirectX 11 or DirectX 12 option because some players’ crashes and performance problems may be tied to the API. Neither choice is declared universally better. Use a controlled comparison to find the more reliable option on your own PC, preserve a baseline, and avoid risking a valuable dungeon run while you test.

sections.heading: Start with the symptom you are trying to solve
paragraphs: Before changing the graphics API, decide whether your problem is a crash, a long loading screen, a visible hitch, unstable frame pacing, or a low average frame rate. Those symptoms are related but not interchangeable. A game that crashes during a transition needs a different observation from a game that runs continuously but stutters when entering a new room. Write down where the problem occurs and whether it began after the version 1.0 release or after a later driver change.

Use a save and route that you can repeat without risking a full backpack. If the issue happens while returning to Tresna, test that transition from a low-value run. If it happens in combat, choose a familiar room and avoid taking rare loot. This makes the comparison both safer and easier to interpret. Do not use a single crash-free session as proof that the problem is permanently gone; repeat the same action several times before calling the result stable.

sections.heading: Record a baseline before switching APIs
paragraphs: Write down the current DirectX selection, display resolution, window mode, frame cap, graphics preset, upscaling option, GPU driver version, and whether the game is installed on an SSD. These are practical context fields, not claims that every one causes the same issue. Keep the graphics options unchanged while you compare APIs. If you update a driver, change a frame cap, and switch APIs together, you will not know which change affected the outcome.

Choose one repeatable scenario: load the same area, follow the same path, trigger the same transition, or perform the same number of combat actions. If the problem is intermittent, use a short series of repeated runs and count how often it appears. Record the time to reach the area only if loading is the symptom you are measuring. A simple log with date, API, scenario, and result is more useful than a broad note that the game “felt smoother.”

sections.heading: Change the API and restart cleanly
paragraphs: Select the alternate DirectX option in the game’s settings and follow any restart prompt. Close the game fully before relaunching if the setting requires a restart. Then repeat the baseline scenario with the same save and unchanged graphics options. Watch for the original symptom first. A higher frame-rate counter does not settle a crash test, and a crash-free route does not prove that a visual hitch improved.

Run the scenario more than once because the first pass after switching may include shader or asset work. If the game requests a shader cache rebuild, let it finish before comparing later runs. Keep the first API result even if it is worse; you need both sides of the comparison to choose responsibly. If the alternate API fails to launch, switch back using the supported settings or launcher flow rather than editing unrelated game files.

sections.heading: Separate stutter from a loading freeze
paragraphs: A brief hitch during movement can be frame pacing, shader compilation, storage activity, or a world transition. A loading screen that never completes is a different failure. Note whether input still responds, whether the transition eventually finishes, and whether the same spot reproduces the issue. Hotfix 1 specifically addressed a tutorial loading-screen freeze while returning to Tresna; do not assume a freeze in every chapter is the identical bug.

For a stutter test, traverse the same small route twice after the initial load. For a freeze test, use the exact return transition and record whether it hangs on both APIs. Do not interrupt a normal loading screen too quickly, but do not leave a repeatable hard freeze unreported. If only one API reproduces it, note that result with the machine and driver details. If both do, the cause may lie elsewhere in the configuration or build.

sections.heading: Interpret results without overclaiming
paragraphs: If DirectX 11 reduces the same crash or stutter on repeated runs, use it as the current workaround on your PC and keep a note of the build. If DirectX 12 behaves better, the same advice applies in reverse. If the results are mixed, choose the option that avoids the more disruptive failure and test again after the next patch. The hotfix asks players with instability or poor performance to try both; it does not publish a winner or a benchmark for every GPU.

Do not compare two different areas or saves and attribute the outcome solely to the API. Enemy count, effects, camera, and loading state can all change the workload. Do not publish an exact frame-rate gain unless you measured it with the same settings and a repeatable scene. Community experiences help identify patterns, but one player’s stable configuration cannot guarantee another system will behave the same way.

sections.heading: What to include in a useful PC report
paragraphs: If the issue persists, include your CPU and GPU models, driver version, Windows version, memory, storage type, selected API, resolution, graphics preset, and a short reproduction path. Say whether the problem is a crash, a permanent freeze, a temporary hitch, or a performance drop. Mention whether it happens on both DirectX options and whether it began before or after Hotfix 1. A clear report is more actionable than a screenshot of a settings menu alone.

Preserve crash details and do not upload private account data or unrelated files. If the game shows an official report form or prompt, use that channel and describe the steps in plain language. Avoid changing save data while investigating a rendering problem. If you need to return to your previous configuration, restore the recorded API and graphics settings one at a time.

sections.heading: Keep a stable play setup after testing
paragraphs: Once one API completes your normal route reliably, keep it selected for the next session and avoid retuning every setting. Stability matters more than chasing a small unverified counter increase when you are carrying valuable loot. If a later patch changes rendering behavior, repeat the same scenario instead of assuming today’s result will remain final. Keep the test note with its date and build so older advice does not look like a universal PC requirement.

The DirectX selector is a useful diagnostic because it offers two supported paths through the same game. Its value comes from a controlled trial: baseline, switch, repeat, compare, and preserve the result. That method helps distinguish an API-specific issue from a broader loading, storage, driver, or save problem without inventing a one-size-fits-all fix.

moonlighter-2-relic-loot-guide.title: Moonlighter 2 Relic and Loot Guide: What to Record
moonlighter-2-relic-loot-guide.description: A Moonlighter 2 relic and loot guide for version 1.0 players tracking item categories, backpack risk, sale observations and unknown values.
moonlighter-2-relic-loot-guide.intro: Moonlighter 2’s core loop turns dungeon loot into shop decisions. A useful relic log is more than a list of names: it connects the item you carried, the route that produced it, the risk you accepted, and what happened when you offered it in Tresna. The released store description confirms relic collection, a backpack puzzle, player-set prices, customers, and village investment, but it does not provide a complete item-price database. This guide gives you a repeatable way to build your own reliable record without treating a single sale as a universal price.

sections.heading: Build a record you can reproduce
paragraphs: Start each entry with the exact item name as the current build displays it. Add the date and version, the dungeon or region, and whether you found it in a normal room, a special encounter, or another identifiable situation. Do not rely on a nickname that only makes sense to you; names make later comparisons searchable. If the same item appears with a quality or modifier, preserve that distinction instead of folding it into one generic row.

Next record the backpack arrangement that brought the item home. Moonlighter’s inventory is part of the run puzzle, so note adjacent items or curse interactions when they changed what you could safely carry. You do not need to capture every move. Record the layout only when it affected your choice, such as leaving an item behind, moving a risky relic, or using a scarce space for something you expected to sell quickly.

Finally separate what you expected from what happened. An observed customer reaction and completed sale are evidence; your estimate before placing the item is a hypothesis. Keep both fields. This lets you refine your pricing later without rewriting the reason you made the first choice. A small log with clear labels is more useful than a large table where observation and guesswork have blended together.

sections.heading: Keep prices tied to their shop context
paragraphs: The released game lets you set prices, and customers communicate their response. A sale amount therefore belongs to a context: the item, your asking price, the customer response, the shop state, and the build. Record the actual price you posted and the response you saw before changing it. If a customer rejects or accepts a price, describe that result rather than translating it into a percentage rule unless you have tested the same item across enough conditions.

Do not copy a price from one item to another because the objects share a broad category such as relic, material, or treasure. A category label is useful for sorting, but it does not prove identical demand or value. Nor does one successful sale establish a perfect price. It establishes that the displayed amount worked in that instance. Use a second comparable sale to check the pattern, and preserve unusual shop conditions as notes rather than silently treating them as noise.

If you change decorations, perks, shop capacity, or another town feature between observations, note the change. Otherwise the next row may look like a price test when it actually compares two different shop states. Where the game does not expose a numeric modifier, simply name the visible change and avoid inventing its effect. A carefully bounded observation can still help another player even when the underlying formula is not published.

sections.heading: Plan the backpack around a real objective
paragraphs: Before entering a dungeon, decide what would make the run worthwhile: a needed crafting component, a category of relic, a safer route test, or simply enough stock to restock the shop. That objective gives backpack space a job. Without one, it is easy to fill every slot with tempting finds and discover that you cannot make a safe decision when the route becomes dangerous.

Treat space, position, and risk together. A relic that is awkward to arrange may be less valuable to this run than an easy-to-carry item you can safely bring home. If an item takes the place of something else, write down that trade. The best inventory plan is not necessarily the layout that holds the greatest theoretical value; it is the layout that leaves you able to respond to what the next room demands.

At each meaningful decision point, compare what is already secured with what the next room could add. If the current haul supports your next shop or village goal, leaving can be a productive choice. The game’s loop connects dungeon returns with selling and reinvestment; a deeper route is useful only when its added opportunity is worth the additional exposure. Link this judgment to your extraction checklist rather than inventing a universal item count or room limit.

sections.heading: Use the run as a controlled test
paragraphs: When learning an unknown value, change one thing at a time. Keep the item, asking price, shop state, and version visible in your note. If you test a new price and also upgrade the shop, you cannot tell which change explains the customer reaction. A good test does not need laboratory precision; it needs enough context that you can avoid attributing a result to the wrong cause.

Separate a route experiment from a sale experiment. On a route test, the question might be whether a particular branch is worth the extra risk. Record the entrance, the decision point, the haul, healing or resources spent, and how you exited. On a sale test, focus on posted price and reaction. This keeps dungeon notes from burying the economy evidence, while still allowing each item row to link back to the run that found it.

Repeat uncertain observations in a later run before promoting them to a recommendation. A single unusually favorable outcome may be memorable without being typical. If your next result disagrees, retain both records and mark the conclusion unresolved. That honesty is especially valuable after patches, when the previous result may have been correct for an older build but no longer describe the current one.

sections.heading: Track loss and upgrade use as outcomes
paragraphs: A relic does not have to reach the shop to matter. If it was lost, discarded to make room, or committed to an upgrade, record that outcome. Those decisions expose the opportunity cost of carrying it. An empty field can mean “not tested”; it should not be converted into a zero value. Use explicit states such as found, extracted, sold, lost, discarded, or used so later readers know what the row actually says.

When you spend a material or relic on an upgrade, record the upgrade name and the reason. This helps distinguish an item that was not sold because it had little demand from one that was intentionally used to progress. It also lets you compare future runs against a concrete goal: did the material unlock something that improved the shop or your next trip? The guide hub’s items tracker, prices page, and shop guide serve different purposes, so use the one that matches the question you are investigating.

Do not let a hypothetical sale price erase the value of a completed upgrade. Gold is one part of the merchant loop, not its only outcome. When you compare routes, include progress toward equipment and village services, along with items sold and losses avoided. The best route for one goal may not be the best route for another, and your notes should make that difference visible.

sections.heading: Version your conclusions
paragraphs: Put the game version or a clear observation date beside every changing value. If you cannot identify the exact build, say that. Update notes should not silently overwrite older runs: preserve the old observation, add a new one, and explain whether the new result confirms or replaces the old conclusion. This is how a guide remains useful when a patch changes a system or when you return to a save after time away.

When a mechanic is not described in official material, label the statement as a test result rather than official behavior. The public listing confirms the broad dungeon, relic, shop, and village loop. It does not publish a complete price chart, item-by-item customer preference table, or exact loss formula. That boundary is useful: readers can act on verified structure while knowing which numbers they should test in their own version.

If you share a correction, include the displayed item name, version, asking price, reaction, and relevant shop state. A screenshot can resolve a spelling or interface question, while a sequence of comparable observations is needed for an economic rule. Strong evidence makes a shared price guide more valuable than another unsourced list of exact-looking numbers.

sections.heading: A compact field-note template
paragraphs: Use one line for each meaningful result, then add detail only when an exception matters. This keeps the note usable during a run and comparable later. A practical entry can include: date/build; item name and quality; source room or route; backpack decision; target or posted price; customer response; sale outcome; upgrade use or loss; shop state; and confidence. Leave unknown values blank and label them unknown instead of guessing.

sections.heading: Turn the notes into a better next run
paragraphs: At the start of the next session, review only the open questions that could change a decision. If you already know which item to carry for a planned upgrade, do not spend the whole run retesting it. Choose one unresolved route or price question, set the conditions you will keep constant, and decide what evidence would change your mind. After returning, update the item log and link the observation to your extraction note. The result is a practical loop: prepare around a goal, collect without overcommitting, sell or invest, and carry the result into the next trip.
