walkthrough.title: Moonlighter 2 Progression Walkthrough and Postgame Priorities
walkthrough.description: A spoiler-aware Moonlighter 2 walkthrough framework for the version 1.0 build, with story and route findings reserved for hands-on verification.
walkthrough.intro: This walkthrough hub is intentionally a framework until the game version and route data are recorded. Steam confirms the starting premise and progression loop, and the version 1.0 announcement confirms the main story now has an ending — but neither publishes a quest order or the ending itself.

sections.heading: Published premise
paragraphs: The player starts without money alongside other townsfolk, stranded in Tresna. The stated goal is to rebuild the shop into the village’s economic center while exploring dungeons, collecting relics, and reinvesting in the community.
bullets: Starting situation: stranded in the distant village of Tresna.
Progression loop: dungeon loot to shop sales to town and equipment upgrades.
Long-term challenge: the Endless Vault tests merchants through escalating trials.
Version 1.0 conclusion: new quests, cutscenes and discoveries bring Will’s journey to an end, followed by the Infinite Endless Vault postgame.

sections.heading: Choosing a difficulty
paragraphs: Difficulty in Moonlighter 2 is mostly about how much relic risk you carry out of a run. On Easy, Normal and Hard, dying halves the quality of every relic in your backpack; on Expert you lose those relics outright; and on Hardcore, added in Version 1.0, a death ends the whole save and you start over. Pick the mode that matches how much you are willing to lose when a run goes wrong — read the current difficulty description before committing valuable progress.
bullets: Easy / Normal / Hard: death halves backpack relic quality.
Expert: death loses the relics in your backpack.
Hardcore (1.0): death loses your progress and restarts the save.

sections.heading: Picking your first weapon
paragraphs: There are four melee classes — Short Swords, Large Swords, Spears and Gauntlets — plus a gun that rides alongside your melee weapon. New players are steered to the Merchant’s Sword: fast, balanced, and the weapon most creators used for early money runs. Swap to the Aetherium Heart or an Ultimate aspect once you can craft one. Whatever you carry, use the gun to knock flying enemies out of the air and keep one bullet in reserve for enemies winding up aerial attacks.

sections.heading: Reading the combat HUD
paragraphs: Each melee class has its own meter to watch: Short Swords chain into a Special Finisher after three hits, Large Swords spend and rebuild Sharpness, Spears plant spearheads the Special recalls, and Gauntlets fill a Berserk gauge. Your gun’s ammo refills slowly on its own and faster when you land melee hits.
bullets: Weapon meter: the class resource (Finisher, Sharpness, spearheads or Berserk).
Ammo: refills on melee hits and breakables; keep one shot in reserve.
Rupture: an enemy at half health turns purple and can be launched with the backpack — but elites and minibosses never rupture.
Tomo’s Radar: the branching node map (chests, events, potions, blacksmith, elite, miniboss, boss, perk rooms) you pick a path through.

sections.heading: Getting potions and healing
paragraphs: Eris, at the Witch Hut, sells potions, health and dungeon perk unlocks, and her riddles point to hidden weapon recipes. Creator guides agree she is the first vendor to upgrade: in the opening hours a reliable healing option matters more than raw damage, so buy more and stronger potions before you invest in weapons.

sections.heading: Managing the shop
paragraphs: The loop is dungeon loot to shop sales to upgrades. Sell relics for gold, then reinvest: Ms. Scratch raises your shop level, K33P3R adds permanent merchant bonuses and Haggle customers, and the Countess sells showcases that raise the price of a whole relic rarity. Nothing you buy in Tresna is lost on death, so shop upgrades are always safe investments — unlike the relics you carry in your backpack.

sections.heading: What still needs a playable build
paragraphs: Exact quest order and the story ending are added only when they can be reproduced first-hand; balance and layout can still shift across post-launch patches, so each step keeps a version note.

sections.heading: Postgame Guide: What to Do After Version 1.0
paragraphs: Moonlighter 2 version 1.0 released on September 2, 2026 and adds a postgame rather than ending the loop at the final story scene. The clean route is to finish the story, choose a new challenge, and keep the shop and dungeon records versioned.

sections.heading: Finish the main story first
paragraphs: The Infinite Endless Vault unlocks after the main story. Finish that route before judging the postgame, because the Vault is explicitly framed as the next stage of the merchant-and-dungeon loop.

sections.heading: Pick one postgame goal
paragraphs: Choose between an Endless Vault threshold, a Hardcore file, an Endless Weapon Aspect test, the Bomb Path, Shop Level 5 or boss and achievement cleanup. Trying to measure all of them in one first postgame run makes the result hard to reproduce.
bullets: Endless Vault: one-run gold thresholds with resets on a failed threshold.
Weapons: four named Endless Weapon Aspects.
Perks: the Bomb Path hit-count explosion loop.
Shop: Level 5 adds a Bloblet slot and a cosmetic placement slot.
Challenge: Hardcore Mode uses the harsher launch-day death wording.

sections.heading: What is still not a public database
paragraphs: The 1.0 announcement does not publish gold thresholds, damage values, boss routes, item prices, shop costs or a save-transfer rule. Those are excellent hands-on article topics, but they should be added only after a build-specific test rather than copied as precise numbers.

sections.heading: The numbers
bullets: Story ending exists in 1.0.

sections.heading: Use the journal as the next-step authority
paragraphs: When two guides describe different stages, compare their save context before changing your route. This walkthrough is a progression framework rather than a substitute for the quest journal. Read the active objective, identify the town service or dungeon it points toward, and complete that specific task before assuming you need a rare drop or a full equipment replacement. A detour is worthwhile when it solves a known resource shortage; it is less useful when it is based on an achievement percentage or an outdated launch checklist.

sections.heading: Campaign Is Only Half the Game
paragraphs: The story ending and optional postgame are separate goals. After the ending, inspect newly available objectives and choose whether to pursue the Vault or an unfinished equipment goal. The amount of content remaining depends on your save rather than a fixed completion percentage.

sections.heading: Will — the player character
paragraphs: Will is the merchant-dungeoner you play, and version 1.0 is built around finishing his arc: the launch post describes "the conclusion of the main story" that brings "Will’s journey in Tresna to its conclusion." Hotfix 1 names Will in its spearhead projectile correction.

sections.heading: Tresna — the town
paragraphs: Tresna is the settlement the whole loop runs on: the launch post frames the whole adventure as exploring Tresna and the vault beneath it, and Hotfix 1 fixes a tutorial freeze "when returning to Tresna," confirming it as the hub you move between dungeon runs.

dungeons-kalina.title: Moonlighter 2 Kalina: Day and Night Realm Encounters
dungeons-kalina.description: Kalina in Moonlighter 2: a desert dimension with the Burn and Armor relic curse. Floors, bosses, unlock quests, route and extraction tips.
dungeons-kalina.intro: Kalina is a desert dimension in Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault, running the Burn and Armor relic curse across two floors. This guide covers both floors, their bosses and unlock quests, how a run is routed, and how to extract safely.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Kalina is one of Moonlighter 2's three dimensions, a desert region with two floors — an easier first floor and a harder second floor. Its relic curse is Burn and Armor: burning relics are destroyed unless an Armored relic sits next to them.

sections.heading: Floors, bosses and how they unlock
bullets: Day Realm (Tier 1) — boss The Herald; minibosses Dafest and Garr'x. Insects and beetles, with bear-trap floors. Unlocks: Open from the start — the tutorial drops you here.

Night Realm (Tier 1) — boss Thalaam; minibosses Hajji and Punkest. Faster night variants of the Day Realm enemies with more health. Unlocks: Quest 'Old Times, New Technology', which starts after your first Herald kill.

sections.heading: Route and how a run works
bullets: Tomo's Radar shows each floor as a branching map of nodes — chests, events, potions, blacksmith, recipe, elite, miniboss, boss, and Ice or Thunder perk rooms — and you pick one branch at every step.
Combat pedestals hand out run perks; stacking one path (all Thunder, all Ignite) beats mixing, and one perk on the gun plus one on the weapon is the usual split.
Chests appear after chest nodes, minibosses and bosses: a few Common relics plus a choice between two higher-rarity ones, with node colour on the radar setting relic quality.
Rupture: an enemy at half health turns purple and can be launched with the backpack into walls, other enemies or off the edge. Elites and minibosses never rupture.

sections.heading: Extraction and death
bullets: The pendant teleports you home at any time with everything in the bag. There is no penalty beyond the loot you skipped, and 'Back to Tresna' relic effects trigger on the way out.

Death penalty by difficulty: on Easy, Normal and Hard every relic in your backpack loses half its quality; on Expert you lose the relics outright; on Hardcore (added in 1.0) you lose your progress and start over.
Because floors unlock through Tresna story quests rather than levels, extract and bank progress freely — you are never grinding XP, only relics and materials.

sections.heading: Drops and materials
paragraphs: Each Kalina boss drops a rare crafting material and two chests, and each floor's two minibosses drop the material for Kalina's early weapon upgrades. Nou and Anacard, at the Silent Exchange, will swap surplus miniboss materials for boss materials.

sections.heading: Dafest Miniboss (Guardian of Disco-Hell)
paragraphs: Dafest, the Guardian of Disco-Hell, is one of the two minibosses on Moonlighter 2's Kalina – Day Realm floor. It appears at the halfway point of the run and drops Broken Microphone.

bullets: Title: Guardian of Disco-Hell.

sections.heading: How to beat it
paragraphs: Dafest spawns with two or three helpers. Kill the helpers first: taser and stun effects wear off much faster on the miniboss itself, so clearing the adds makes the crowd control stick.
Elites and minibosses do not enter the Rupture state, so the backpack throw only works on their adds, not on the miniboss.

paragraphs: The Herald is a 3-phase Moonlighter 2 realm boss at the end of Kalina's Day Realm. The first boss in the game. Beating him the first time starts the quest that opens the Night Realm.

sections.heading: Attack patterns and phases
bullets: Starts every phase behind 6 energy shields. Catch the purple bomb blobs with your backpack and throw them back to strip the shields.

Phase 2 destroys the right-hand cover and adds a two-way laser.

Kalina bosses reward dodge discipline: bring a maxed short sword and focus on reading telegraphs over raw burst.
Learn the telegraphs first — every attack has a wind-up you can dodge — and make sure your weapon is upgraded before you commit a farming run.

sections.heading: Route and how a run works
bullets: Tomo's Radar shows each floor as a branching map of nodes — chests, events, potions, blacksmith, recipe, elite, miniboss, boss, and Ice or Thunder perk rooms — and you pick one branch at every step.
Combat pedestals hand out run perks; stacking one path (all Thunder, all Ignite) beats mixing, and one perk on the gun plus one on the weapon is the usual split.
Chests appear after chest nodes, minibosses and bosses: a few Common relics plus a choice between two higher-rarity ones, with node colour on the radar setting relic quality.
Rupture: an enemy at half health turns purple and can be launched with the backpack into walls, other enemies or off the edge. Elites and minibosses never rupture.

bullets: The pendant teleports you home at any time with everything in the bag. There is no penalty beyond the loot you skipped, and 'Back to Tresna' relic effects trigger on the way out.

weapons.description: A source-tracked Moonlighter 2 weapons and upgrades guide based on official equipment categories and village progression.
weapons.intro: Moonlighter 2 has four melee classes — Short Swords, Large Swords, Spears and Gauntlets — plus a gun that rides alongside your melee weapon and a set of armor. Every class has a Merchant’s starter, an Ultimate version, named Early Access aspects, a Boss Rush aspect from the Blob-Life update, and an Endless aspect from Version 1.0. This page indexes every weapon with its special effect, how to unlock it, and where it fits.

sections.heading: How the weapon classes work
bullets: Short Swords: three arcing slashes and an Attack Finisher; the Special is a spin that chains into a Special Finisher after three hits.
Large Swords: wide slashes that spend Sharpness; the Special rebuilds it, and damage scales with the current Sharpness level.
Spears: quick stabs that plant spearheads; the Special recalls every spearhead, hitting everything in their path.
Gauntlets: rapid punches that fill the Berserk meter; the Special slams both gauntlets and Berserk raises damage and attack speed.
Guns: built at Babyl’s Workshop, ammo refills on melee hits, and shots knock flying enemies out of the air.

sections.heading: Choose the reference that matches the decision
paragraphs: The family references separate short swords, large swords, spears and gauntlets so that a crafting question does not require reading every equipment entry at once. Start with the family you already use comfortably. Compare the recipe shown in your installed build with the resources you actually have, then decide whether the purchase solves a concrete problem on your current route. A named weapon entry is a description of an option, not a promise that it outranks every alternative.

Keep weapon choice separate from the rest of the loadout when comparing attempts. A run with different armor, perks and gadgets cannot tell you precisely how much the weapon changed the result. If you want to understand an upgrade, keep the route familiar and pay attention to attack commitment, reach and whether you can reposition safely. Damage potential matters only when you can use it. The gadget comparison covers ranged options separately, and the armor guide covers survivability spending; use those pages when the actual problem lies outside the melee weapon.

sections.heading: Compare upgrades with a specific route
paragraphs: Before purchasing an upgrade, choose the route or encounter that the purchase is meant to improve. Keep your armor, perks and input method familiar during the first comparison. Inspect the item description before and after the upgrade and record the change that actually appears. Then try the same kind of opening rather than judging the new weapon from a single large hit. If the upgrade makes a risky commitment more attractive but does not solve recovery, the route may still require a shorter attack sequence. If your existing weapon already clears ordinary rooms comfortably, supplies or a service relevant to the active objective may be a more useful next expense. Preserve an affordable fallback until the new setup behaves predictably.

moonlighter-2-hardcore-mode.title: Moonlighter 2 Difficulty and Hardcore: Death Rules and Preparation
moonlighter-2-hardcore-mode.description: Moonlighter 2 Hardcore Mode explained: the launch-day wording, the earlier relic-loss wording, and the safer way to start a file.
moonlighter-2-hardcore-mode.intro: Moonlighter 2 version 1.0 includes Hardcore Mode. The launch-day announcement says dying means losing progress and starting from the very beginning, while an earlier announcement described losing relics on defeat. Because the two official wordings differ, the safe assumption is the harsher one.

sections.heading: The current Hardcore wording
paragraphs: The September 2 launch post describes death as losing progress and starting the journey again from the very beginning. That is the wording attached to the build that shipped with version 1.0.

sections.heading: Why older guides disagree
paragraphs: The August 5 announcement described Hardcore Difficulty as losing all relics upon defeat in the Moonlighter style. Losing relics and restarting the whole journey are different penalties, and neither announcement explains the difference. This page keeps both statements visible instead of silently choosing one.

note.label: Practical rule
note.text: Until the in-game description or a later patch note clarifies the difference, assume a defeat can erase the run from the beginning.

sections.heading: Who should start Hardcore first?
paragraphs: Use a normal file to learn the shop, dungeon, relic and extraction loop before committing a Hardcore run. If you do start immediately, keep an offline save backup only for technical recovery; do not use it to claim that the mode has a different in-game death rule.

sections.heading: Difficulty and Death: What You Lose on Each Setting
paragraphs: Moonlighter 2 does not make enemies spongier as the difficulty rises. It changes what a death takes from your backpack — and on one setting, from your save. Pick the setting by how much you want a bad run to cost.

sections.heading: The death penalty ladder
paragraphs: Every difficulty uses the same dungeons and the same relic curses. The difference is what happens to the bag when you go down.
bullets: **Easy, Normal and Hard** — every relic in your backpack loses half its quality
**Expert** — you lose the relics outright
**Hardcore** (added in version 1.0) — you lose your progress and start over

sections.heading: Which to pick
paragraphs: **Normal** is the setting the loop is tuned for. Half quality on a death stings enough to make extraction a real decision, without turning one bad room into an evening.
**Expert** changes how you route rather than how you fight: losing the relics outright makes every extra node a wager, so you pendant out earlier and run shorter, richer loops.
**Hardcore** is a second-playthrough mode. Its wording is a progress loss, not a relic loss — treat it as a separate campaign, not a difficulty tweak on your main save.

sections.heading: What difficulty does not change
paragraphs: Use the active story objective and available region access to plan progression. A difficulty choice and a quest unlock answer different questions. Before switching modes, read the current description and whether the change applies to the current save or a new one; do not assume that every setting preserves town upgrades or vendor progress.
That asymmetry is the whole strategy: **spend before you explore**. Coins turned into potions, a shop level or a vendor unlock cannot be lost. Relics in the backpack always can.
bullets: Sell the bag before you upgrade
Hardcore mode
Autosave and sleeping

sections.heading: Where the game sits now
paragraphs: The recurring criticism in the negative pile is grind rather than difficulty — which is another way of saying the death penalty, not the enemy health bar, is what people are actually reacting to.

sections.heading: Do Not Test DirectX on a Hardcore File
paragraphs: Hotfix 1 added a switch between DirectX 11 and DirectX 12 because crashes were tied to that choice. Hardcore, added in version 1.0, can end the save. Test the API on a file you can lose an evening on, not on the file you cannot lose at all.

sections.heading: Two switches
paragraphs: The API switch is a graphics menu. Try both. Keep the one that finishes a load back to Tresna. Minimum spec hints at DirectX 11. Recommended hints at DirectX 12. A recommended GPU can still prefer DX11 if that is the crash this hotfix was written for.

Hardcore is a progress loss, a separate campaign. Easy, Normal, and Hard halve backpack quality. Expert deletes the relics. Practicing a DX toggle or a Kalina hole on Hardcore deletes the file you were using to learn. Use the file that keeps the town.

sections.heading: Retest after the API holds
paragraphs: Walk the Kalina out-of-map spot once. Talk to Hazy Jane if input used to die. Unequip Scarabastion and fight a boss before you call that armor best. Retest a distant shot on Sergeant Roberto if the gun felt blank. Do not enable Hardcore to see if the gun is serious.
bullets: The API test
Sell on the safe file
Hardcore wording

sections.heading: Disk and console
paragraphs: Use troubleshooting instructions appropriate to the platform. A Windows graphics-API option should not be assumed to exist on another device. When reporting a freeze, identify the platform, installed build, storage type and the transition where it occurs. Confirm that a low-risk test finishes reliably before returning to a high-stakes save.

sections.heading: Make a mode decision before a build decision
paragraphs: Choose difficulty around the type of session you want. Learning unfamiliar routes and checking a risky mechanic are different activities from attempting a long-term survival challenge. A player who wants to understand a new weapon may benefit from practicing outside a mode where failure has a larger consequence. That is a preparation choice, not a claim that the harder option contains better loot. Read the mode description in the current build before creating a save and do not assume a backup will be restored automatically after a loss.

If a technical issue makes the game unreliable on your machine, investigate stability before committing to a high-consequence save. Difficulty and the graphics API solve different problems. Reducing combat pressure does not diagnose a crash, and selecting a different renderer does not change the mode’s stated death rule.

moonlighter-2-infinite-endless-vault-gui.title: Moonlighter 2 Endless Vault: Challenge Preparation and Run Planning
moonlighter-2-infinite-endless-vault-gui.description: How the Moonlighter 2 Infinite Endless Vault works after the main story, including single-run gold thresholds, resets and confirmed reward categories.
moonlighter-2-infinite-endless-vault-gui.intro: The Infinite Endless Vault is the version 1.0 postgame in Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault. It unlocks after the main story and turns the merchant loop into increasingly difficult gold thresholds that must be completed in one run.

sections.heading: How the Endless Vault works
paragraphs: The launch announcement describes an endless series of increasingly difficult thresholds. Each threshold must be completed in a single run, and failing to reach its required amount of gold resets progress for that threshold. Partial gold progress does not bank between attempts.

sections.heading: What the Vault rewards
paragraphs: The confirmed reward categories are equipment, shop upgrades, decorations and cosmetics. The announcement does not publish a threshold count, exact gold target, scaling formula or final depth, so a guide should not fill those fields with a guessed number.
bullets: Unlock: complete the main story.
Run rule: each threshold is completed in one run.
Failure: falling short of the gold requirement resets that threshold.
Rewards: equipment, shop upgrades, decorations and cosmetics.

sections.heading: A safe first attempt
paragraphs: Treat the first run as a route test. Record the vault stage, relic categories, backpack pressure, shop return decision and gold target shown by the build. Push only as far as you can extract without turning a valuable haul into an avoidable reset.

sections.heading: Two Boons Per Run
paragraphs: Reviews that like the 1.0 combat call out the two-boon limit as the thing that keeps a run readable. It is a constraint, not a bug.

sections.heading: Pick before the second region
paragraphs: One boon for the weapon you are actually swinging. One for the problem that region has, usually sustain or a bomb angle. A third idea belongs to the next run.
Endless Weapon Aspects are a different system. Do not stack a boon plan and an aspect plan and then blame the shop when the bag is nonsense.
bullets: Weapon aspects

sections.heading: Moonlighter 2: Only Two Boons per Run
paragraphs: Two boons per run is the limit players keep naming, and it is why a six-region loop stays readable. A third offer is a replacement, not a stack. Endless Weapon Aspects are a different system. Do not plan a boon and an aspect as if they share a slot.

sections.heading: Pick for the room you are about to enter
paragraphs: If the next node on Tomo’s Radar is an elite or a miniboss, take the boon that answers that room. A damage boon you cannot trigger before the pendant is wasted. A defensive boon on a run you already mean to extract is also wasted.
Elites and minibosses do not rupture. The backpack launch is for a normal enemy at half health, the one that turns purple. Do not save a boon for a rupture on a boss.
bullets: Two boons
Elite telegraphs
Endless Weapon Aspects

sections.heading: Separate the challenge from the preparation run
paragraphs: The Endless Vault is part of the game’s progression loop rather than a reason to ignore your shop. The store description connects its challenges to town upgrades and increasingly valuable rewards. That tells you what the system is for, but it does not establish a universal loadout or a guaranteed payout for every attempt. Start by reading the current challenge prompt in your own save. Treat its displayed requirement as the target and prepare around that requirement rather than around someone else’s completed save.

Before committing, check what resources you are putting at risk and what you need afterward. If an attempt would consume the resources you need to recover from a failure, do a normal earning run first. This is a budgeting recommendation, not a hidden entry restriction. A useful preparation run can leave you with stock, materials or a familiar combat rhythm even when it does not advance the challenge itself. Calling every preparation run wasted time makes the next attempt harder to fund.

Use equipment you understand. An unfamiliar aspect, gadget or perk combination may have greater theoretical potential but still perform worse for you when you have not learned its timing. Test one change on a familiar route before taking it into a demanding objective. If it changes your ability to stop, reposition or deal with a group, adjust your plan before investing more resources. Keep the challenge attempt focused on execution rather than on learning every system simultaneously.

After a failure, identify the decision that ended the attempt. Was the target misunderstood, the budget too tight, the inventory poorly prepared, or a fight handled carelessly? Each answer calls for a different correction. Repeating the same expensive setup without identifying the failure point is not a progression strategy. Return when you can state what you will do differently. For the spending calculation itself, use the threshold-budget route; for reward expectations, use the separate rewards guide instead of assuming every stage gives the same return.

sections.heading: Know what success should unlock
paragraphs: After a successful challenge, read the result and inspect the town services before planning the next attempt. A completed objective can change what you are able to buy or improve, and that new opportunity may matter more than repeating the previous route immediately. Preserve the difference between an announced feature and a reward you have personally received. If your save does not show the expected progression, check its current quest state and build before treating the discrepancy as a hidden requirement.

bosses.title: Moonlighter 2 Bosses and Ultimate Challenge Preparation
bosses.description: Moonlighter 2 bosses: the Curator, Senda, Tyke and Monte are the four bosses Steam confirms by name, ordered by how many players have actually beaten each one.
bosses.intro: Prepare for Moonlighter 2 boss encounters by matching your destination, equipment and run objective. This directory connects the realm guides with a practical preparation checklist. Achievement rarity is not a recommended fight order or a measure of a boss’s damage.

sections.heading: The six realm bosses by floor
paragraphs: Each of the three dimensions has two floors, and each floor ends in a boss. Every realm boss drops a rare crafting material and two chests; each floor also has two minibosses at the halfway point that drop the material for that dimension’s early weapon upgrades.
bullets: The Herald — Kalina, Day Realm; 3 phases; drops Sound of Harmony.
Thalaam — Kalina, Night Realm; 3 phases; bell-throwing shield fight.
The Curator — The Gallery, Exhibition Wing; 3 phases; drops Quantum Core.
Tyke — The Gallery, Treasury Halls; 3 phases; frees a captured friend.
Senda — Aeolia, Zephyr Fields; 2 phases; drops The King’s Left Mask.
Monte — Aeolia, Howling Harbor; 3 phases; rated the hardest realm boss.
All twelve minibosses and Moloch, the story finale.

sections.heading: Who Moloch is
paragraphs: Moloch is not a realm boss on the Kalina / Gallery / Aeolia floors. He is the story antagonist you confront after clearing the six realm bosses and reaching the Endless Vault, and Version 1.0 builds Will's ending around him.
bullets: Positioned as the interdimensional collector who stole your homeland.
The realm bosses (The Herald, Thalaam, The Curator, Tyke, Senda, Monte) come first; Moloch caps the story.

sections.heading: The final fight
paragraphs: Community boss guides describe Moloch as a three-phase fight — telegraphed melee in phase one, zone-control bursts in phase two, and room-wide attacks in phase three — cleared with a maxed gauntlet or sword, healing relics, and a practised dodge. Digital Sun has not published an official phase breakdown, and the two community sources differ on specifics, so treat the phase details as player-reported rather than confirmed.

sections.heading: Boss Completion Guide: How to Track Progress
paragraphs: Moonlighter 2’s Steam achievement data provides a useful completion signal for bosses, while the public store material does not provide a complete boss route, health table or universal weapon recommendation. Track each named encounter with the same versioned method.

sections.heading: Separate boss completion from the main story
paragraphs: A boss defeat can be a story milestone, a Steam achievement, an Endless Vault test or a personal route objective. Log which kind it is. Completing the main story does not automatically prove that every postgame challenge or named encounter is complete.

sections.heading: The checklist fields that matter
paragraphs: For each boss, record the displayed name, location or dungeon label, weapon and relic setup, whether the run was normal or Hardcore, and the date or version. Add the reward only after it is visible in the build.

sections.heading: Avoid a fake best-build answer
paragraphs: The launch data confirms weapons, armor, gadgets and village upgrades as progression categories, but it does not publish a complete boss weakness or damage ranking. Test one variable at a time and describe a build as suitable for a specific encounter rather than universally best.

sections.heading: Prepare for a boss without inventing a recommended level
paragraphs: Begin with the destination. The realm guides below collect the named encounters for Kalina, the Gallery and Aeolia, so you can distinguish a floor boss from a miniboss and find the relevant preparation notes. Do not use an achievement percentage to decide the correct fight order. Unlock conditions, player preferences and the age of a save can all change those percentages. Your quest journal and the route available in your current save are better starting points.

Build around attacks you can finish safely. A weapon is useful when you can enter a damage window, complete the attack and move before the next threat. If you repeatedly take damage while recovering, try a shorter commitment or a more conservative opening before spending materials on a larger damage number. This does not imply that every boss requires the same weapon class. It gives you a way to compare your own attempts without pretending there is one universal best setup.

Use early attempts to recognize the dangerous transitions. When a fight changes its arena, adds another source of pressure or interrupts your usual rhythm, stop treating the previous pattern as a complete script. Spend a moment learning what is newly unsafe. Avoid converting a single successful dodge into a guaranteed timing rule. Input, position and the combination of threats all affect whether a response works. Your goal is to find a repeatable opening with enough margin to recover from a mistake.

Check the result after the fight rather than assuming a fixed reward table. Read the displayed item names, the quest update and any newly available town services. Materials that look interchangeable may serve different recipes. Keep a note of what actually arrived in this save and compare it with the crafting menu before selling or spending it. Challenge clears and campaign encounters can serve different purposes, so a reward observed in one context should not be copied into every encounter entry.

If a fight behaves incorrectly, separate the bug from the strategy problem. A stuck enemy, missing transition or unresponsive room should be recorded with the build, platform and encounter name. Updating and reproducing the case is more useful than inventing an invisible phase condition. The hotfix guide describes documented progression fixes; the stuck-enemy recovery guide explains how to report an unresolved encounter while minimizing unnecessary save changes.

sections.heading: Moloch Final Boss
paragraphs: Use the active story objective to establish whether you are ready to continue the final encounter. Check equipment, available resources and difficulty before entering. Do not infer the required order from global achievement percentages.

prices.title: Moonlighter 2 Prices and Inventory: A Practical Selling Worksheet
prices.description: Plan Moonlighter 2 shop prices with a selling worksheet for your own asking prices, customer reactions and item outcomes.
prices.intro: Use a repeatable selling routine in Moonlighter 2: sort the haul, set an asking price, read customer responses, then reinvest in the next run. This page combines the price worksheet with the inventory decisions that make a sale possible. It does not provide a universal item-price database.

sections.heading: What a trustworthy price entry needs
paragraphs: A price number without context is easy to misread. The same item may need a test note for its source, shop state, event state, customer reaction, and game version. This guide will keep those fields visible so a reader can distinguish a measured observation from a community lead.
bullets: Item name exactly as displayed
Starting price or first observed sale price
Customer reaction at the tested price
Where the item was acquired
Game version and test date

sections.heading: How to use the table after launch
paragraphs: Start with one item and record a small price range rather than claiming one universal best number. Then compare the result after shop upgrades or special events. The store page says special events can affect sales momentum, so event context belongs in the data row.

sections.heading: Items and Relics
paragraphs: Steam confirms that dungeon runs produce relics and that the player sells loot to develop the shop and village. The complete names, stats, drop tables, and values need a playable data pass before they can be called a reliable item list.

sections.heading: Confirmed item role
paragraphs: The official store description uses relics, loot, battered scrap, weapons, armor, gadgets, shop decorations, and perks as the building blocks of the adventure-and-merchant loop. It also says value is not fixed by a published universal price: the player decides the sale price.
bullets: Relics and other loot come from dungeon exploration.
Weapons, armor, and gadgets are listed as unlockable equipment categories.
Shop decorations and perks are part of shop progression.
Village investment is tied to better equipment and upgrades.

sections.heading: Relic Curses: Burn, Shock and Petrify Explained
paragraphs: Each of the three dimensions puts a different curse on the relics you pick up, and the curse is why the backpack is a puzzle instead of a list. Pack wrong and the relic you crossed a floor for is destroyed before you reach the pendant.

sections.heading: One dimension, one curse
paragraphs: The curse is a property of the dimension, not of the relic. Walk into Kalina and everything you pick up plays by Burn and Armor rules; walk into The Gallery and the same slot behaves completely differently.
That means the packing habit you built in your first dimension actively hurts you in the second. Re-learn the grid each time you unlock a new region.
bullets: Kalina — desert, Tier 1
The Gallery — museum machines, Tier 2
Aeolia — witches and storms, Tier 3

sections.heading: Kalina — Burn and Armor
paragraphs: A burning relic is destroyed unless an **Armored** relic sits next to it. Armor is not loot you are saving for later; it is the firewall you build the rest of the bag around.

Practical rule: never let a burning relic take a slot that has no Armored neighbour. If you only have one Armored relic, you only have room for one burning relic, no matter how much empty space is left.

sections.heading: The Gallery — Shock and Overcharge
paragraphs: A shocked relic becomes **Overcharged** and gains quality — which makes this the one curse you can farm deliberately. Shock it a second time and it explodes, unless a **Battery** drains it.

So the Gallery bag is a risk ladder: one shock is a free upgrade, two is a loss, and a Battery is what turns the second shock back into a profit. Carry the Battery before you start chasing Overcharge.

sections.heading: Aeolia — Petrify and Absorb
paragraphs: Petrified relics become **Aetherium crystals**, and other relics **Absorb** those crystals for quality. Leftover Aetherium is destroyed when the run ends, so an unabsorbed crystal is a wasted slot.
That makes Aeolia the dimension where extraction timing is a quality decision, not just a safety one. Finish the absorbing before you pull the pendant, or you carry home a bag of nothing.

sections.heading: How to pack any of them
paragraphs: Decide the curse interaction at the moment you pick a relic up, not at the exit. Every one of these three systems punishes a bag you planned to sort later.
Elites and bosses do not rupture, so you cannot clear space with a backpack launch mid-fight. The space you have at the door is the space you fight with.
bullets: The backpack is the puzzle
When to extract
Relic and loot guide

sections.heading: Backpack: The Puzzle Is the Bag
paragraphs: The currency counter in the corner goes up. The bag does not. That tension is the game. A review that wants a bigger bag is asking for a different game.

sections.heading: What to drop
paragraphs: Drop the relic you cannot price tonight. A famous item you will undercharge is worse than a small item you know.
Hotfix 1 did not add a bag expansion. Shop Level 5 changes the store, not the dungeon grid.
bullets: Items
Prices

sections.heading: Use the worksheet without mistaking it for live market data
paragraphs: The price worksheet is a personal record of the amount you choose to ask and what happens afterward. It is not connected to your save or to a server collecting other players’ prices. Enter the item name exactly as shown, keep different qualities separate, and add enough shop context that a later comparison makes sense. A price accepted once is a useful observation, but it is not proof that the amount is the maximum every customer will pay.

When evaluating a sale, compare like with like. Change the asking price while keeping the item and shop state as similar as practical. If you buy a decoration, activate a perk or encounter a special event, record it before comparing the new result with an older sale. The official description confirms customer responses and shop modifiers, so ignoring those conditions can turn a genuine observation into a misleading price rule. The aim is a useful selling decision, not a precision formula the game has not published.

beginner-guide.description: A fact-first Moonlighter 2 beginner guide covering dungeon runs, relics, shop prices, and village reinvestment.
beginner-guide.intro: Start Moonlighter 2 by completing one manageable cycle: enter a dungeon with a clear goal, bring relics home, sell stock in Tresna, and use the proceeds to improve the next trip. This guide explains the decisions between those steps so your first sessions produce useful progress rather than repeated resets.

sections.heading: Start with the two-role loop
paragraphs: Steam presents the game as an action RPG with roguelike elements. You leave the village to explore dangerous dungeons, gather relics, return with a backpack of loot, and sell that loot in your shop.
bullets: Treat a dungeon run as a risk-and-reward trip, not only a combat stage.
Keep the shop step connected to the run: loot has no value to your progress until it is sold or used for an upgrade.
Reinvest in the village because the Steam description links a growing village with better weapons, armor, upgrades, and new people.

sections.heading: What to record on the first real run
paragraphs: The Steam page confirms the systems, but it does not publish a complete item database. On the first playable run, record the item name, where it came from, the displayed sale price, customer reaction, and whether the result changed after an upgrade or event.

sections.heading: The clean progression order
paragraphs: A sensible recording order follows the official loop: survive a dungeon, sort relics, test one price, sell, then check which village investment or equipment option became available. This is a workflow recommendation, not an unverified claim about the strongest build.

sections.heading: Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault Gameplay Preview
paragraphs: Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault connects an action-RPG dungeon run to a player-run shop and village. This preview uses the Steam listing and the official version 1.0 announcements while leaving exact prices, routes, and combat values for a reproducible build check.

sections.heading: The gameplay loop in one sentence
paragraphs: Steam describes a loop of exploring dangerous dungeons, gathering relics and loot, returning to the shop, setting prices, reading customers, and reinvesting in the village. That is the most reliable answer to “what is Moonlighter 2 gameplay?”: the adventure and merchant roles are designed to feed each other.
bullets: Dungeon run: explore, fight, and collect relics.
Shop step: arrange loot, set a price, and read customer reactions.
Progression step: reinvest in the village, weapons, armor, upgrades, and shop systems.
Challenge step: push farther into the Endless Vault for greater risk and reward.

sections.heading: Why pricing is part of the gameplay
paragraphs: The official store description says the player sets their own price and reads customers to find the right deal. Steam does not publish a universal item-price chart, so a useful guide should record the item name, acquisition source, displayed reaction, shop state, event context, and game version rather than inventing a formula.

sections.heading: What version 1.0 added to that loop
paragraphs: Version 1.0 released on September 2, 2026 and extended the loop at both ends. The main story now concludes, and past that ending the Infinite Endless Vault turns the challenge step into a gold-target ladder: each threshold has to be cleared in a single run, and falling short of the required gold resets progress on that threshold. The launch post also names four Endless Weapon Aspects, Shop Level 5, the Bomb Path perk path, Hardcore Mode, and new vendors, cosmetics and Codex pages. Those names are confirmed; their damage, prices, unlock conditions and gold targets are not published anywhere.

sections.heading: A clean first-session test
paragraphs: On a real build, keep the first comparison controlled: note the dungeon depth, relic category, backpack state, return decision, sale price, customer reaction, and village option unlocked afterward. Then repeat one variable at a time. That produces a useful gameplay guide without mixing Early Access observations, community claims, and 1.0 marketing copy.

sections.heading: What this preview does not claim
paragraphs: The official sources do not provide a complete item database, exact dungeon map, boss route, weapon tier list, price formula, or save-transfer rule. Those are good search intents, but they need a versioned hands-on entry on the 1.0 build rather than a guess based on the store description.

sections.heading: Inventory — Why Reviews Call It a Weak Point
paragraphs: A review that calls the game cute and the combat precise still names inventory management and the ending as the bad points. Official copy never publishes a backpack size. Extraction is the design answer: leave before the bag is a puzzle you hate.

sections.heading: A first-session plan you can actually finish
paragraphs: Choose one achievable objective before starting a run. Early on, that might be understanding how your equipped weapon recovers after an attack, returning with stock for the shop, or seeing which town service the current quest wants you to visit. Avoid combining a new route, a new weapon and a risky purchasing decision in the same attempt. If the attempt goes badly, you want to know which choice needs changing. A short successful cycle teaches more than a long attempt where the cause of failure is unclear.

In the dungeon, watch how much safety you spend to collect each additional piece of loot. A room that leaves you badly hurt has a different cost from one you clear comfortably, even when the chest looks similar. Arrange the backpack before pressing forward rather than waiting for a dangerous choice to expose an awkward inventory. Keep the goal in sight: bringing a modest haul back gives you something to sell, and selling creates the next set of decisions in Tresna.

At home, separate selling from shopping for upgrades. Check what you brought back, what the next available purchase asks for, and whether that purchase solves the problem you encountered. If you were being caught during attacks, a more expensive weapon is not automatically the solution; practicing the recovery window may be more useful. If stock is accumulating without helping your budget, spend a session understanding customers and your asking prices before making the next large investment.

Finish the session with one concrete next step. Write down the town service, recipe, quest objective or route you intend to work on. You do not need a perfect build or a complete database to make progress. You need a cycle you can repeat and a clear reason for changing it. The shop guide covers selling decisions; the dungeon guide covers route and encounter choices; the equipment references help when the crafting menu presents several plausible upgrades.

sections.heading: Merchant's Sword — Short Sword Guide
paragraphs: Merchant's Sword is a short sword in Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault, added in Early Access. The effect is tied to a Special Finisher. Inspect the current description for the bonus and duration, then compare whether the encounter gives you time to use the follow-up safely.

sections.heading: Special effect
paragraphs: The effect is tied to a Special Finisher. Inspect the current description for the bonus and duration, then compare whether the encounter gives you time to use the follow-up safely.
bullets: Class: Short Sword.
Class mechanic: Short Swords land three arcing slashes and an Attack Finisher. The Special is a full-circle spin that can be chained into a Special Finisher after three normal hits.
Added: Early Access.

sections.heading: How to get
paragraphs: Starter craft at Andrei's Forge.

sections.heading: Best use
paragraphs: The balanced beginner short sword and the weapon most creators used for early money runs. Keep it until you find an Ultimate aspect or the Aetherium Heart.

sections.heading: Everlasting Fury — Short Sword Guide
paragraphs: Everlasting Fury is a short sword in Moonlighter 2: The Endless Vault, added in Early Access. Its role is a finisher-focused option for tougher encounters.
